passage_text: Researchers at the University of Midvale conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of three different cognitive training programs on reaction time in adults aged 35–55. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, Treatment A (visual-spatial drills), Treatment B (verbal memory drills), and a Combined group that received both types of drills. Each participant completed a standardized reaction time task before and after a 4‑week intervention period. The table below summarizes the average reaction times (in seconds) and standard deviations for each group immediately post‑intervention. The researchers hypothesized that the Combined group would exhibit the greatest improvement, followed by Treatment A, then Treatment B, with the control group showing minimal change. Their findings were intended to inform the design of workplace training programs aimed at enhancing cognitive performance.
stem: Which group demonstrated the fastest average reaction time immediately after the intervention?
explanation: The table shows the Combined group with the lowest average reaction time of 0.589 seconds, indicating the fastest performance among all groups.
trap: The distractor that often misleads students is the Control group, which actually had the slowest reaction time.

stem: Which experimental design element best supports causal inference that the training caused the observed changes in reaction time?

options.C: Use of a standardized reaction time task

explanation: Correct: Random assignment makes the groups comparable at the start, so differences afterward can be attributed to the training. Why the others are wrong: A) restricting age narrows the population but does not make groups comparable. C) a standardized task improves measurement consistency, not internal validity. D) reporting SDs describes spread but does not control confounding.
trap: Students often choose the use of a standardized task (C) because it seems to control measurement error, but it does not address internal validity.

trap: Using the wrong baseline or wrong pair of groups; percent improvement is the 0.033 s difference divided by the Control mean (0.645 s).

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: The Combined group had a faster mean reaction time than the Control group.
options.B: Treatment A had a lower average reaction time than Treatment B.
options.C: The Control group had the highest average reaction time.
options.D: The improvement in the Combined group is statistically significant.

explanation: Correct: The table gives post‑intervention means only, with no statistical tests, so significance cannot be claimed. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.589 s is faster than 0.645 s. B) 0.612 s is lower than 0.625 s. C) the Control mean of 0.645 s is the highest.
trap: Accepting 'statistically significant' as supported when only means and SDs are shown and no test or p‑value is reported.

stem: By how many seconds was the mean reaction time of the Combined group faster than that of Treatment A?
explanation: Correct: 0.612 − 0.589 = 0.023 s. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.056 s is the gap between Combined and Control (0.645 − 0.589). C) 0.033 s is the gap between Control and Treatment A. D) 0.020 s is the gap between Control and Treatment B.
trap: Subtracting from the Control mean (0.056 s) instead of from the Treatment A mean as the question asks.
